title: Observability and Operations
summary: Make the system explain what it is doing before an incident forces you to guess.
keyPoints: Metrics show trends, logs explain one event, and traces show the path and timing of a request.
RED covers request-serving services; USE covers resources such as CPU, memory, and queues.
Report p50 with p95 or p99, because averages hide the tail users remember.
An SLO turns reliability into a target, and the error budget guides release and alerting decisions.
Alert on user-facing symptoms with an owner and a runbook, not on every internal cause.
Queue age, dead-letter counts, and worker saturation reveal problems that queue depth alone can hide.

complexity.note: Sampling and retention dominate storage cost.
Merge histograms instead of averaging percentiles.
Structured fields and a request id make search useful.

commonMistakes: Monitoring average latency while the p99 is far above the user-facing target.
Paging on a cause such as CPU usage instead of a symptom such as a failing checkout.
Using unbounded labels like user id or request id in metrics, which explodes cardinality.
Alerting on queue depth without tracking message age or drain time.
interviewNotes: Name the user-facing SLO and the metric that measures it before listing dashboards.
Separate symptom alerts from cause dashboards, and say who gets paged.
Use p95 or p99 with a stated window, and explain why the average is insufficient.
Include queue age, retry rate, and dead-letter depth when the design has asynchronous work.
End with the runbook and incident response: detection, mitigation, rollback, and follow-up.

checkYourself.question: Why is p99 more useful than average latency for a user-facing service?
checkYourself.answer: The average hides slow requests. p99 shows the experience of the slowest group, which is often what users notice and what fan-out amplifies.

checkYourself.question: What is an error budget?
checkYourself.answer: It is the amount of unreliability an SLO allows, such as 0.1% of a 30-day window. It gives the team a shared measure for balancing releases and reliability work.

checkYourself.question: Why can queue depth be a misleading alert?
checkYourself.answer: Depth changes with arrival rate. A stable depth can still mean messages wait too long, so track oldest message age and drain time as well.
